title: Αἰνείας καὶ Ἀχιλλεύς
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Apollo tells Aeneas to pray, since he is the son of Zeus’s daughter Aphrodite and Achilles only of a lesser god, and to carry his bronze straight at him. Aeneas goes through the front fighters, and Hera sees him. She calls Poseidon and Athena together and asks whether to turn Aeneas back or to send a god to give Achilles strength, so that he will know the gods love him; what fate has spun for him will come later, but he should not meet a god unaided. Poseidon says there is no need yet: the gods should sit apart and watch, and join in only if Ares or Apollo begins the fighting or holds Achilles back. Poseidon’s party sits down on Heracles’ old wall, wrapped in cloud, the others on Callicolone around Apollo and Ares, and Zeus bids from on high. The plain fills with armies, and Aeneas and Achilles meet in the space between them. Achilles asks Aeneas what he hopes to gain, reminds him how he once ran from him on Ida and escaped only because the gods saved him, and tells him to go back into the crowd before he suffers for it.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἄναξ Διὸς υἱὸς Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipen anax Dios huios Apollōn·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the lord, the son of Zeus, Apollo:
sentences.i: Then lord Apollo, the son of Zeus, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν is Aeneas, who has just finished speaking, and Apollo, who has been speaking to him in the voice of Lycaon, answers. ἄναξ is ‘lord’ and Διὸς υἱός ‘the son of Zeus’, a title of Apollo that the line completes with his name. προσέειπεν is the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘addressed’, with the epic uncontracted -εε-; αὖτε ‘in turn’ marks a second speech to the same hearer.

sentences.t:
ἥρως ἀλλ’ ἄγε καὶ σὺ θεοῖς αἰειγενέτῃσιν
εὔχεο·
sentences.tr:
hērōs all’ age kai sy theois aieigenetēisin
eucheo·
sentences.l:
“Hero, but come, you too to the gods, the forever-born,
pray;
sentences.i: “Hero, but come, you too, pray to the everlasting gods;
sentences.n: ἥρως ‘hero’ is the address Apollo gives Aeneas. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, and εὔχεο is the present imperative of εὔχομαι, here ‘pray’. αἰειγενέτῃσιν is the epic dative plural (-ῃσιν) of αἰειγενέτης ‘forever-born’, from αἰεί ‘always’ and γίγνομαι ‘be born’, a stock epithet of the gods. Apollo’s speech begins here.

sentences.t:
καὶ δὲ σέ φασι Διὸς κούρης Ἀφροδίτης
ἐκγεγάμεν, κεῖνος δὲ χερείονος ἐκ θεοῦ ἐστίν·
sentences.tr:
kai de se phasi Dios kourēs Aphroditēs
ekgegamen, keinos de chereionos ek theou estin·
sentences.l:
And indeed you they say, of Zeus’ daughter Aphrodite,
to have been born, but that one is from a lesser god;
sentences.i: And indeed they say you were born of Aphrodite, daughter of Zeus, while he is from a lesser god;
sentences.n: καὶ δὲ is ‘and indeed’. φασι ‘they say’ has no named speaker. ἐκγεγάμεν is the epic perfect infinitive of ἐκγίγνομαι ‘be born from’, which takes the genitive Διὸς κούρης Ἀφροδίτης. κεῖνος (= ἐκεῖνος) is Achilles, and χερείονος is the genitive of χερείων ‘lesser, inferior’, itself a comparative form; who the lesser god is the next line says.

sentences.t: ἣ μὲν γὰρ Διός ἐσθ’, ἣ δ’ ἐξ ἁλίοιο γέροντος.
sentences.tr: hē men gar Dios esth’, hē d’ ex halioio gerontos.
sentences.l: for the one is of Zeus, and the other from the old man of the sea.
sentences.i: for the one is a child of Zeus, the other of the old man of the sea.
sentences.n: ἣ μὲν … ἣ δ’ is ‘the one … the other’: Aphrodite, and the mother of Achilles, whom the Greek does not name here. ἐσθ’ is ἐστί with its last vowel elided, and Διός ‘of Zeus’ is a genitive of descent, as is ἐξ ἁλίοιο γέροντος ‘from the old man of the sea’, a sea-god. The English adds ‘child’, which the Greek leaves understood.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἰθὺς φέρε χαλκὸν ἀτειρέα, μηδέ σε πάμπαν
λευγαλέοις ἐπέεσσιν ἀποτρεπέτω καὶ ἀρειῇ.
sentences.tr:
all’ ithys phere chalkon ateirea, mēde se pampan
leugaleois epeessin apotrepetō kai areiēi.
sentences.l:
But straight on bear the unwearied bronze, and not at all you
with pitiful words let him turn away, and with threats.”
sentences.i: But carry the unwearied bronze straight on, and do not let him turn you aside at all with pitiful words and threats.”
sentences.n: ἰθύς ‘straight on’ is an adverb, and φέρε χαλκὸν ἀτειρέα is ‘carry the unwearied bronze’, the bronze being the spear-point that stands for the weapon. μηδέ … ἀποτρεπέτω is a third-person command, ‘let him not turn’; the subject is not named, but the last man spoken of is κεῖνος, Achilles. πάμπαν ‘at all’ strengthens the negative; λευγαλέοις ἐπέεσσιν is ‘with pitiful words’ and ἀρειῇ a rare word for ‘threat’, singular in the Greek, ‘threats’ in the English. Apollo’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἔμπνευσε μένος μέγα ποιμένι λαῶν,
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn empneuse menos mega poimeni laōn,
sentences.l: So having spoken, he breathed great might into the shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and breathed great might into the shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes Apollo’s speech; the subject of ἔμπνευσε is Apollo. ἔμπνευσε is the aorist of ἐμπνέω ‘breathe into’, and μένος is the ‘might’ a god puts into a fighter. ποιμένι λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ is a stock title of a leader, and here it is Aeneas.

sentences.t: βῆ δὲ διὰ προμάχων κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ.
sentences.tr: bē de dia promachōn kekorythmenos aithopi chalkōi.
sentences.l: and went through the front-fighters, armed with the fire-faced bronze.
sentences.i: and he went through the foremost fighters, armed with bronze that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: The subject of βῆ is Aeneas, the ‘shepherd of the people’ of the line before. πρόμαχοι ‘front-fighters’ are the men who fight in the van. κεκορυθμένος is the perfect passive participle of κορύσσω ‘arm’ (from κόρυς ‘helmet’), and αἴθοπι, from αἴθοψ ‘fiery’, literally ‘fire-faced’, goes with χαλκῷ.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἔλαθ’ Ἀγχίσαο πάϊς λευκώλενον Ἥρην
ἀντία Πηλεΐωνος ἰὼν ἀνὰ οὐλαμὸν ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.tr:
oud’ elath’ Anchisao païs leukōlenon Hērēn
antia Pēleïōnos iōn ana oulamon andrōn·
sentences.l:
Nor did Anchises’ son escape white-armed Hera,
going against the son of Peleus up through the crowd of men;
sentences.i: Nor did the son of Anchises escape the notice of white-armed Hera as he went against the son of Peleus up through the crowd of men;
sentences.n: In οὐδ’ ἔλαθ’ Ἀγχίσαο πάϊς λευκώλενον Ἥρην the subject is Ἀγχίσαο πάϊς ‘Anchises’ son’, Aeneas, and Hera is the object: λανθάνω with the accusative is ‘escape the notice of’. Ἀγχίσαο is the epic genitive in -αο. ἀντία Πηλεΐωνος ‘against the son of Peleus’ names Achilles by his father, and ἀνὰ οὐλαμόν is ‘up through the crowd’, οὐλαμός being a throng or press of men.

sentences.t: ἣ δ’ ἄμυδις στήσασα θεοὺς μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.tr: hē d’ amydis stēsasa theous meta mython eeipe·
sentences.l: And she, having made the gods stand together, among them spoke a speech:
sentences.i: She gathered the gods together and spoke among them:
sentences.n: ἣ is Hera. στήσασα is the aorist participle of ἵστημι in its causal sense, ‘having made stand’, and with ἄμυδις ‘together’ it is ‘having drawn the gods up together’, the gods who have come down to the battle. μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπε is the stock introduction ‘spoke a speech among them’, with μετά meaning ‘among them’.

sentences.t:
φράζεσθον δὴ σφῶϊ Ποσείδαον καὶ Ἀθήνη
ἐν φρεσὶν ὑμετέρῃσιν, ὅπως ἔσται τάδε ἔργα.
sentences.tr:
phrazesthon dē sphōï Poseidaon kai Athēnē
en phresin hymeterēisin, hopōs estai tade erga.
sentences.l:
“Take thought now, you two, Poseidon and Athena,
in your wits, how these deeds shall be.
sentences.i: “Take thought now, the two of you, Poseidon and Athena, in your wits, how these things are to turn out.
sentences.n: φράζεσθον is a dual imperative of φράζομαι ‘take thought’, and σφῶϊ is the dual pronoun ‘you two’; both name Poseidon and Athena, who are addressed in the vocative (Ποσείδαον is the vocative of Ποσειδάων). ὑμετέρῃσιν is ‘your’, in the epic dative -ῃσιν. ὅπως ἔσται τάδε ἔργα is an indirect question, ‘how these deeds will be’, that is, how this will turn out. Hera’s speech begins here.

sentences.t:
Αἰνείας ὅδ’ ἔβη κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ
ἀντία Πηλεΐωνος, ἀνῆκε δὲ Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.tr:
Aineias hod’ ebē kekorythmenos aithopi chalkōi
antia Pēleïōnos, anēke de Phoibos Apollōn.
sentences.l:
This Aeneas has gone, armed with the fire-faced bronze,
against the son of Peleus, and Phoebus Apollo has urged him on.
sentences.i: Here is Aeneas, who has gone out against the son of Peleus, armed with bronze that has the look of fire, and Phoebus Apollo has urged him on.
sentences.n: ὅδ’ is ὅδε ‘this’, the pronoun for what is near; Hera points to Aeneas as he comes into view. κεκορυθμένος αἴθοπι χαλκῷ is the phrase of the line where he set out. ἀντία Πηλεΐωνος ‘against the son of Peleus’ is Achilles. ἀνῆκε, the aorist of ἀνίημι, is ‘urged on’, with Aeneas understood as its object; Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων names the god behind the move.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’, ἡμεῖς πέρ μιν ἀποτρωπῶμεν ὀπίσσω
αὐτόθεν·
sentences.tr:
all’ ageth’, hēmeis per min apotrōpōmen opissō
autothen·
sentences.l:
But come, let us ourselves turn him away backward
from this very spot;
sentences.i: But come, let us ourselves turn him back from this very spot;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ is the plural of ἀλλ’ ἄγε ‘but come’. ἀποτρωπῶμεν is a subjunctive used as an exhortation, ‘let us turn away’; ἀποτρωπάω is a form of ἀποτρέπω ‘turn aside’, and μιν ‘him’ is Aeneas. ἡμεῖς πέρ ‘we ourselves’, ὀπίσσω ‘backwards’, and αὐτόθεν ‘from this very spot’.

sentences.t:
ἤ τις ἔπειτα καὶ ἡμείων Ἀχιλῆϊ
παρσταίη, δοίη δὲ κράτος μέγα,
sentences.tr:
ē tis epeita kai hēmeiōn Achilēï
parstaiē, doiē de kratos mega,
sentences.l:
or else let some one of us then also beside Achilles
stand, and give him great strength,
sentences.i: or else let one of us stand beside Achilles and give him great strength,
sentences.n: ἤ ‘or’ brings the second choice: either turn Aeneas back, or help Achilles. παρσταίη (aorist optative of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’, with παρ- cut from παρα-; Attic παρασταίη) and δοίη (aorist optative of δίδωμι ‘give’) are optatives of wish used as exhortations, ‘let one stand … and give’. ἡμείων is the epic genitive plural of ἡμεῖς ‘of us’. κράτος is ‘strength’, a word that may include the upper hand.

sentences.t:
μηδέ τι θυμῷ
δευέσθω,
sentences.tr:
mēde ti thymōi
deuesthō,
sentences.l:
and let him not in any way in his heart
be lacking,
sentences.i: and let him lack nothing in his heart,
sentences.n: μηδέ continues the command with a negative: ‘and let him not’. δευέσθω is the third-person singular imperative of δεύομαι ‘lack, be in want’; τι ‘in any way’ and θυμῷ ‘in his heart’ say in what respect. The subject is still Achilles, and ‘lack in heart’ means be short of spirit.

sentences.t:
ἵνα εἰδῇ ὅ μιν φιλέουσιν ἄριστοι
ἀθανάτων,
sentences.tr:
hina eidēi ho min phileousin aristoi
athanatōn,
sentences.l:
so that he may know that him love the best
of the immortals,
sentences.i: so that he may know that the best of the immortals love him,
sentences.n: ἵνα εἰδῇ is ‘so that he may know’, a purpose clause with the subjunctive of οἶδα. ὅ is a neuter relative used as the conjunction ‘that’. φιλέουσιν is the uncontracted φιλέω ‘love’ (Attic φιλοῦσιν), and ἄριστοι ἀθανάτων is ‘the best of the immortals’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ αὖτ’ ἀνεμώλιοι οἳ τὸ πάρος περ
Τρωσὶν ἀμύνουσιν πόλεμον καὶ δηϊοτῆτα.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ aut’ anemōlioi hoi to paros per
Trōsin amynousin polemon kai dēïotēta.
sentences.l:
and that those, in turn, are empty, who even before now
ward off war and fighting for the Trojans.
sentences.i: and that those who until now have been warding off war and fighting from the Trojans are empty.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ αὖτ’ ἀνεμώλιοι continues the ὅ-clause of the unit before: ‘and that those, in turn, are empty’. ἀνεμώλιος ‘empty’, from ἄνεμος ‘wind’, means of no effect. The ones meant are the gods who have so far protected the Trojans: οἳ τὸ πάρος περ Τρωσὶν ἀμύνουσιν, ‘who even before now ward off … for the Trojans’, with ἀμύνω ‘ward off’ taking the accusative of what is warded off, πόλεμον καὶ δηϊοτῆτα ‘war and fighting’, and the dative of those protected.

sentences.t:
πάντες δ’ Οὐλύμποιο κατήλθομεν ἀντιόωντες
τῆσδε μάχης,
sentences.tr:
pantes d’ Oulympoio katēlthomen antioōntes
tēsde machēs,
sentences.l:
And all from Olympus we came down, meeting
this battle,
sentences.i: And we have all come down from Olympus to meet this battle,
sentences.n: πάντες … κατήλθομεν is ‘we all came down’: Hera speaks for all the gods who have come to the plain. Οὐλύμποιο is the epic genitive in -οιο. ἀντιόωντες is the participle of ἀντιάω ‘meet’, which takes the genitive μάχης, so ‘meeting’ or ‘taking part in’ this battle, with τῆσδε ‘this’ pointing at the fighting about to begin.

sentences.t:
ἵνα μή τι μετὰ Τρώεσσι πάθῃσι
σήμερον·
sentences.tr:
hina mē ti meta Trōessi pathēisi
sēmeron·
sentences.l:
so that he may not suffer anything among the Trojans
today;
sentences.i: so that he may come to no harm among the Trojans today;
sentences.n: ἵνα μή gives the purpose of coming down: ‘so that he may not’. The subject is not named; it is Achilles, who is the object of the plan. πάθῃσι is the subjunctive of πάσχω ‘suffer’, and μή τι πάθῃσι ‘not suffer anything’ is a mild way to say come to harm. μετὰ Τρώεσσι is ‘among the Trojans’.

sentences.t:
ὕστερον αὖτε τὰ πείσεται ἅσσά οἱ αἶσα
γιγνομένῳ ἐπένησε λίνῳ ὅτε μιν τέκε μήτηρ.
sentences.tr:
hysteron aute ta peisetai hassa hoi aisa
gignomenōi epenēse linōi hote min teke mētēr.
sentences.l:
Later, in turn, he will suffer those things, as many as for him his portion
spun with the thread as he was being born, when his mother bore him.
sentences.i: But later he will suffer whatever his lot spun for him with the thread when he was born, when his mother bore him.
sentences.n: τὰ … ἅσσα is ‘those things … as many as’. αἶσα is ‘lot’, the portion given to each man, and ἐπένησε is the aorist of ἐπινέω ‘spin to’: the picture is of a thread spun for a man when he is born, with λίνῳ ‘with the thread’ a thread of flax. γιγνομένῳ ‘as he was being born’ is a present participle agreeing with οἱ ‘for him’. The ‘he’ is Achilles, and what the lot holds is not said.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ Ἀχιλεὺς οὐ ταῦτα θεῶν ἐκ πεύσεται ὀμφῆς
δείσετ’ ἔπειθ’,
sentences.tr:
ei d’ Achileus ou tauta theōn ek peusetai omphēs
deiset’ epeith’,
sentences.l:
But if Achilles will not learn these things from the voice of the gods,
he will be afraid then,
sentences.i: But if Achilles does not learn this from the voice of the gods, then he will be afraid,
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ … οὐ ‘but if … not’ is followed by the future πεύσεται (πεύθομαι ‘learn’). ταῦτα ‘these things’ points back to what the gods mean to tell him: that they love him and stand by him. ὀμφή is a voice with a god behind it, and θεῶν ἐκ … ὀμφῆς is ‘from the voice of the gods’, with ἐκ standing between the two words. δείσετ’ is δείσεται, the future of δείδω ‘fear’, with its last vowel elided, and ἔπειθ’ is ἔπειτα ‘then’.

sentences.t:
ὅτε κέν τις ἐναντίβιον θεὸς ἔλθῃ
ἐν πολέμῳ·
sentences.tr:
hote ken tis enantibion theos elthēi
en polemōi·
sentences.l:
whenever some god head-on comes
in war;
sentences.i: whenever some god comes at him head-on in war;
sentences.n: ὅτε κέν … ἔλθῃ is ‘whenever … comes’, with the subjunctive for what may happen. τις θεός is ‘some god’, any god. ἐναντίβιον ‘head-on’ is literally ‘against his strength’, and ἐν πολέμῳ ‘in war’ says where; the ‘him’ in the English is Achilles.

sentences.t: χαλεποὶ δὲ θεοὶ φαίνεσθαι ἐναργεῖς.
sentences.tr: chalepoi de theoi phainesthai enargeis.
sentences.l: and hard are gods to appear, manifest.”
sentences.i: for gods are hard when they appear in manifest form.”
sentences.n: χαλεποί ‘hard’ is the word for what is hard to bear or to deal with; φαίνεσθαι, the infinitive of φαίνομαι ‘appear’, says in what respect: when they appear. ἐναργεῖς ‘manifest’ means a god showing himself openly, in his own form, not disguised. Hera’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Poseidaōn enosichthōn·
sentences.l: Her then answered Poseidon earth-shaker:
sentences.i: Then Poseidon earth-shaker answered her:
sentences.n: τὴν is Hera. ἠμείβετ’ is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, with its last vowel elided, and ἔπειτα ‘then’: the stock formula that introduces a reply. ἐνοσίχθων is built from ἐνόσις ‘shaking’ and χθών ‘earth’, so ‘earth-shaker’, Poseidon’s epithet.

sentences.t: Ἥρη μὴ χαλέπαινε παρ’ ἐκ νόον· οὐδέ τί σε χρή.
sentences.tr: Hērē mē chalepaine par’ ek noon· oude ti se chrē.
sentences.l: “Hera, do not grow harsh beyond sense; nor is there any need for you.
sentences.i: “Hera, do not be angry beyond reason; you have no need to be.
sentences.n: μὴ χαλέπαινε is a prohibition with the present imperative of χαλεπαίνω ‘grow harsh, be angry’. παρ’ ἐκ, printed as two words, is παρέκ ‘out beyond’, here with the accusative νόον ‘mind’, so ‘beyond what the mind allows’, unreasonably. οὐδέ τί σε χρή is ‘nor is there any need for you’; the verb χρή is impersonal. Poseidon’s speech begins here.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν ἔγωγ’ ἐθέλοιμι θεοὺς ἔριδι ξυνελάσσαι
ἡμέας τοὺς ἄλλους, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτεροί εἰμεν·
sentences.tr:
ouk an egōg’ etheloimi theous eridi xynelassai
hēmeas tous allous, epei ē poly pherteroi eimen·
sentences.l:
I at least would not wish to drive the gods together in strife,
us the others, since indeed much stronger we are;
sentences.i: I for one would not want to drive the rest of us gods together into strife, since we are, in truth, far stronger;
sentences.n: οὐκ ἂν … ἐθέλοιμι is ‘I would not wish’ (optative with ἄν), and ἔγωγ’ ‘I for my part’. ξυνελάσσαι is the aorist infinitive of συνελαύνω ‘drive together’ with the old spelling ξυν-, and ἔριδι ‘in strife’ says into what. θεούς … ἡμέας τοὺς ἄλλους is ‘the gods, us the others’ (ἡμέας is the Ionic ἡμᾶς), so Poseidon counts himself among the gods he means. φέρτεροί εἰμεν ‘we are stronger’ (εἰμεν = ἐσμέν) gives no ‘than’; the Greek leaves the comparison to the hearer.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἡμεῖς μὲν ἔπειτα καθεζώμεσθα κιόντες
ἐκ πάτου ἐς σκοπιήν, πόλεμος δ’ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει.
sentences.tr:
all’ hēmeis men epeita kathezōmestha kiontes
ek patou es skopiēn, polemos d’ andressi melēsei.
sentences.l:
but let us, for our part, then sit down, going
out of the path to a lookout, and war will be the care of men.
sentences.i: But let us, for our part, go off the path to a lookout and sit down there, and war will be the concern of men.
sentences.n: καθεζώμεσθα is the subjunctive of καθέζομαι ‘sit down’, used as an exhortation, and κιόντες (from κίω ‘go’) says how: ‘going’. ἐκ πάτου is ‘out of the path’, πάτος being a trodden way, and ἐς σκοπιήν ‘to a lookout’, a place from which one watches. πόλεμος δ’ ἄνδρεσσι μελήσει is a plain future, ‘war will be the care of men’ (ἄνδρεσσι, the epic dative plural), the words of 6.492.

sentences.t: εἰ δέ κ’ Ἄρης ἄρχωσι μάχης ἢ Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων,
sentences.tr: ei de k’ Arēs archōsi machēs ē Phoibos Apollōn,
sentences.l: But if Ares begin the battle, or Phoebus Apollo,
sentences.i: But if Ares or Phoebus Apollo should start the battle,
sentences.n: εἰ δέ κ’ … ἄρχωσι is ‘but if … begin’, with κε and the subjunctive; the verb is plural because both Ares and Apollo are its subject. ἄρχω with the genitive μάχης is ‘begin’ the battle. Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is the stock name and epithet.

sentences.t: ἢ Ἀχιλῆ’ ἴσχωσι καὶ οὐκ εἰῶσι μάχεσθαι,
sentences.tr: ē Achilē’ ischōsi kai ouk eiōsi machesthai,
sentences.l: or hold Achilles back and do not allow him to fight,
sentences.i: or hold Achilles back and will not let him fight,
sentences.n: Ἀχιλῆ’ is Ἀχιλῆα with its last vowel elided, with a single λ for the metre. ἴσχωσι is the subjunctive of ἴσχω ‘hold back’, and εἰῶσι the subjunctive of ἐάω ‘allow’; the subjects are still Ares and Apollo, and the ‘if’ of the line before governs both.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα καὶ ἄμμι παρ’ αὐτόθι νεῖκος ὀρεῖται
φυλόπιδος·
sentences.tr:
autik’ epeita kai ammi par’ autothi neikos oreitai
phylopidos·
sentences.l:
at once then for us too, right there, a quarrel will rise
of the din of battle;
sentences.i: then at once, for us too, a quarrel of the din of battle will rise there on the spot;
sentences.n: αὐτίκ’ is αὐτίκα ‘at once’. ἄμμι is the epic dative of ἡμεῖς, ‘to us’, and παρ’ αὐτόθι is ‘right there, on the spot’. νεῖκος ‘quarrel’ is the subject of ὀρεῖται, the future of ὄρνυμι in the middle, ‘will arise’, and the genitive φυλόπιδος ‘of the din of battle’ says what kind: a quarrel carried on in battle.

sentences.t:
μάλα δ’ ὦκα διακρινθέντας ὀΐω
ἂψ ἴμεν Οὔλυμπον δὲ θεῶν μεθ’ ὁμήγυριν ἄλλων
ἡμετέρῃς ὑπὸ χερσὶν ἀναγκαίηφι δαμέντας.
sentences.tr:
mala d’ ōka diakrinthentas oïō
aps imen Oulympon de theōn meth’ homēgyrin allōn
hēmeterēis hypo chersin anankaiēphi damentas.
sentences.l:
and very quickly, parted, I think,
they will go back to Olympus, to the assembly of the other gods,
subdued under our hands by necessity.”
sentences.i: and I think that they will very quickly be parted and go back to Olympus, to the assembly of the other gods, overcome under our hands by necessity.”
sentences.n: ὀΐω ‘I think’ takes the infinitive ἴμεν (the epic form of ἰέναι ‘to go’), whose accusative subject is left unsaid: ‘them’, Ares and Apollo. διακρινθέντας ‘parted’ (aorist passive of διακρίνω ‘separate’) and δαμέντας ‘subdued, overcome’ (aorist passive of δάμνημι) agree with that unsaid ‘them’; the Greek does not say from what they are parted. Οὔλυμπον δέ is ‘to Olympus’, and μεθ’ ὁμήγυριν ‘to the assembly’. ἀναγκαίηφι is ‘by necessity’, in the instrumental ending -φι. Poseidon’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἡγήσατο κυανοχαίτης
τεῖχος ἐς ἀμφίχυτον Ἡρακλῆος θείοιο
ὑψηλόν,
sentences.tr:
hōs ara phōnēsas hēgēsato kyanochaitēs
teichos es amphichyton Hēraklēos theioio
hypsēlon,
sentences.l:
So then, having spoken, led the way the dark-haired one
to the wall heaped-around of Heracles, divine,
high,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the dark-haired one led the way to the wall of divine Heracles, heaped up around and high,
sentences.n: The subject is Poseidon, whom the Greek does not name here, only by his epithet κυανοχαίτης ‘dark-haired’ (literally ‘dark-maned’); the English keeps it so. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is the stock ‘so then, having spoken’. Ἡρακλῆος is the epic genitive of Ἡρακλῆς and θείοιο is ‘divine’ in the epic -οιο. ἀμφίχυτον is ‘poured’ or ‘heaped up around’ (ἀμφί + χέω ‘pour’), a wall banked up round a place.

sentences.t:
τό ῥά οἱ Τρῶες καὶ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
ποίεον,
sentences.tr:
to rha hoi Trōes kai Pallas Athēnē
poieon,
sentences.l:
which for him the Trojans and Pallas Athena
made,
sentences.i: which the Trojans and Pallas Athena had made for him,
sentences.n: τό is the relative ‘which’, the wall, and οἱ ‘for him’ is Heracles. ποίεον is the imperfect of ποιέω ‘make’ with the epic ending -εον (Attic ἐποίουν); the English ‘had made’ puts it before Poseidon led the way. The story of why they made it is not told here, only what it was for.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα τὸ κῆτος ὑπεκπροφυγὼν ἀλέαιτο,
ὁππότε μιν σεύαιτο ἀπ’ ἠϊόνος πεδίον δέ.
sentences.tr:
ophra to kētos hypekprophygōn aleaito,
hoppote min seuaito ap’ ēïonos pedion de.
sentences.l:
so that the sea-monster, escaping out and away, he might avoid,
whenever it should drive him from the beach to the plain.
sentences.i: so that he might escape from the sea-monster and avoid it, whenever it drove him from the beach to the plain.
sentences.n: ὄφρα … ἀλέαιτο is a purpose clause, ‘so that he might avoid’ (the optative of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’). ὑπεκπροφυγών is a compound of φεύγω with three prefixes, ὑπό ‘from under’, ἐκ ‘out’, πρό ‘forth’: ‘escaping out and away’. κῆτος is a sea-monster. ὁππότε μιν σεύαιτο is ‘whenever it should drive him’, with μιν ‘him’ Heracles and ἠϊόνος the ‘beach’; πεδίον δέ is ‘to the plain’, with -δε for motion towards.

sentences.t: ἔνθα Ποσειδάων κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο καὶ θεοὶ ἄλλοι,
sentences.tr: entha Poseidaōn kat’ ar’ hezeto kai theoi alloi,
sentences.l: There Poseidon sat down, and the other gods,
sentences.i: There Poseidon sat down, and the other gods,
sentences.n: κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο is κατὰ … ἕζετο ‘sat down’, with the preposition cut off from the verb (tmesis) and ἄρα as a connecting particle. θεοὶ ἄλλοι ‘the other gods’ are the gods of Poseidon’s side.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἄρρηκτον νεφέλην ὤμοισιν ἕσαντο·
sentences.tr: amphi d’ ar’ arrēkton nephelēn ōmoisin hesanto·
sentences.l: and around their shoulders an unbreakable cloud they put on;
sentences.i: and wrapped an unbreakable cloud about their shoulders;
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … ἕσαντο is ‘put around themselves’, the aorist middle of ἕννυμι ‘clothe’ with ἀμφί in tmesis. ἄρρηκτον ‘unbreakable’ describes the cloud, and ὤμοισιν is the dative ‘on their shoulders’. The Greek does not say what the cloud is for.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἑτέρωσε καθῖζον ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι Καλλικολώνης
ἀμφὶ σὲ ἤϊε Φοῖβε καὶ Ἄρηα πτολίπορθον.
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ heterōse kathizon ep’ ophrysi Kallikolōnēs
amphi se ēïe Phoibe kai Arēa ptoliporthon.
sentences.l:
But the others sat down on the other side, on the brows of Callicolone,
around you, Ēïe Phoebus, and Ares the city-sacking.
sentences.i: while the others sat down on the other side, on the brows of Callicolone, around you, Phoebus, and Ares, the city-sacker.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘but they’ are the gods of the Trojan side, who sit apart; ἑτέρωσε is ‘to the other side’ and καθῖζον the imperfect of καθίζω ‘sit down’. ὀφρύσι is the dative of ὀφρύς ‘brow’, a hill’s brow or ridge, and Καλλικολώνη, a name that means ‘fair hill’, is a hill. The poet turns to address Apollo: σὲ … Φοῖβε. ἤϊε is a title of Apollo whose meaning is not known: the word-for-word line keeps it as Ēïe, the plain English leaves it out; Ἄρηα πτολίπορθον is ‘Ares the city-sacker’.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μέν ῥ’ ἑκάτερθε καθήατο μητιόωντες
βουλάς·
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men rh’ hekaterthe kathēato mētioōntes
boulas·
sentences.l:
So they, on either side, were sitting, planning
counsels;
sentences.i: So they sat on either side, making their plans;
sentences.n: ὣς … μέν sums up the two parties, ‘so they on either side’. ἑκάτερθε is ‘on either side’, καθήατο the epic imperfect of κάθημαι ‘sit’, and μητιόωντες the participle of μητιάω ‘plan’ (from μῆτις ‘cunning’), with its object βουλάς ‘counsels’, plans.

sentences.t:
ἀρχέμεναι δὲ δυσηλεγέος πολέμοιο
ὄκνεον ἀμφότεροι,
sentences.tr:
archemenai de dysēlegeos polemoio
okneon amphoteroi,
sentences.l:
but to begin the painful war
they shrank, both sides,
sentences.i: but both sides were reluctant to begin the painful war,
sentences.n: ἀρχέμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἄρχω ‘begin’, and ὄκνεον the imperfect of ὀκνέω ‘shrink from, hesitate’, with the epic ending -εον. δυσηλεγέος ‘painful’: the sense is not certain; the word is probably from δυσ- ‘bad’ and the root of ἄλγος ‘pain’, but another derivation, from ἀλέγω ‘heed’, would make it ‘pitiless’. ἀμφότεροι is ‘both sides’.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς δ’ ἥμενος ὕψι κέλευε.
sentences.tr: Zeus d’ hēmenos hypsi keleue.
sentences.l: and Zeus, sitting on high, was bidding.
sentences.i: while Zeus, sitting on high, gave his bidding.
sentences.n: κέλευε is the imperfect of κελεύω ‘bid’; it has no object, so the Greek does not say whom Zeus bids or what. ἥμενος is the participle of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and ὕψι ‘on high’; Zeus has stayed on Olympus.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἅπαν ἐπλήσθη πεδίον καὶ λάμπετο χαλκῷ
ἀνδρῶν ἠδ’ ἵππων·
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ hapan eplēsthē pedion kai lampeto chalkōi
andrōn ēd’ hippōn·
sentences.l:
And of them all the plain was filled, and shone with bronze,
of men and of horses;
sentences.i: And the whole plain was filled with them, men and horses, and shone with bronze;
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of them’ is the armies, and ἀνδρῶν ἠδ’ ἵππων ‘of men and horses’ says who they are. ἐπλήσθη, the aorist passive of πίμπλημι ‘fill’, takes the genitive of what fills, so ‘was filled with them’. λάμπετο is the imperfect of λάμπομαι ‘shine’, and χαλκῷ ‘with bronze’ is their armour.

sentences.t:
κάρκαιρε δὲ γαῖα πόδεσσιν
ὀρνυμένων ἄμυδις.
sentences.tr:
karkaire de gaia podessin
ornymenōn amydis.
sentences.l:
and shook the earth under the feet
of those rushing together.
sentences.i: and the earth shook under their feet as they pressed forward together.
sentences.n: κάρκαιρε is a rare verb whose meaning is not known for certain; ‘shook’ is a guess from the picture of the ground under thousands of feet. πόδεσσιν ὀρνυμένων is ‘under the feet of those rushing’ (the participle of ὄρνυμι in the middle), and ἄμυδις ‘together’.

sentences.t:
δύο δ’ ἀνέρες ἔξοχ’ ἄριστοι
ἐς μέσον ἀμφοτέρων συνίτην μεμαῶτε μάχεσθαι
Αἰνείας τ’ Ἀγχισιάδης καὶ δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr:
dyo d’ aneres exoch’ aristoi
es meson amphoterōn synitēn memaōte machesthai
Aineias t’ Anchisiadēs kai dios Achilleus.
sentences.l:
And two men, far the best,
into the midst of both came together, the two eager to fight,
Aeneas, Anchises’-son, and heavenly Achilles.
sentences.i: And two men, far the best, came together into the space between the two armies, both of them eager to fight, Aeneas, son of Anchises, and heavenly Achilles.
sentences.n: δύο … ἀνέρες ‘two men’ is picked up by the dual verb συνίτην ‘came together’ and the dual participle μεμαῶτε ‘the two eager’ (perfect of μέμαα). ἔξοχ’ ἄριστοι is ‘far the best’ (ἔξοχα ‘above others’, elided). The middle line is repeated from the meeting of Glaucus and the son of Tydeus; ἐς μέσον ἀμφοτέρων is the ground between the two armies. Ἀγχισιάδης is the patronymic ‘son of Anchises’.

sentences.t:
Αἰνείας δὲ πρῶτος ἀπειλήσας ἐβεβήκει
νευστάζων κόρυθι βριαρῇ·
sentences.tr:
Aineias de prōtos apeilēsas ebebēkei
neustazōn korythi briarēi·
sentences.l:
And Aeneas first, having threatened, had set out,
nodding with his weighty helmet;
sentences.i: Aeneas had advanced first, with threats, nodding with his heavy helmet;
sentences.n: ἐβεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω ‘go’, ‘had set out’. ἀπειλήσας, the aorist participle of ἀπειλέω ‘threaten’, says he came with threats; the Greek does not say what they were. νευστάζων is the participle of a rare verb ‘nod’, here with κόρυθι βριαρῇ ‘with his weighty helmet’ (βριαρός, from βρίθω ‘be heavy’) in the dative.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἀσπίδα θοῦριν
πρόσθεν ἔχε στέρνοιο, τίνασσε δὲ χάλκεον ἔγχος.
sentences.tr:
atar aspida thourin
prosthen eche sternoio, tinasse de chalkeon enchos.
sentences.l:
but his impetuous shield
before his chest he held, and he shook the bronze spear.
sentences.i: and he held his impetuous shield in front of his chest and shook his bronze spear.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘and, but’ is an epic conjunction. θοῦριν is the accusative of θοῦρις ‘impetuous, rushing’, agreeing with ἀσπίδα. πρόσθεν … στέρνοιο is ‘in front of the chest’, with the genitive, and τίνασσε is the imperfect of τινάσσω ‘shake’.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐναντίον ὦρτο λέων ὣς
σίντης,
sentences.tr:
Pēleïdēs d’ heterōthen enantion ōrto leōn hōs
sintēs,
sentences.l:
And Peleus’-son from the other side against him rose, like a lion,
a ravager,
sentences.i: And from the other side the son of Peleus rose up against him like a ravaging lion,
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης ‘son of Peleus’ is Achilles. ὦρτο is the aorist of ὄρνυμι in the middle, ‘rose, rushed’, and ἐναντίον ‘against’ him. λέων ὣς is ὡς λέων with the particle after its noun, and the comparison runs to line 173. σίντης ‘ravager’ is from σίνομαι ‘harm’.

sentences.t:
ὅν τε καὶ ἄνδρες ἀποκτάμεναι μεμάασιν
ἀγρόμενοι πᾶς δῆμος·
sentences.tr:
hon te kai andres apoktamenai memaasin
agromenoi pas dēmos·
sentences.l:
whom even men are eager to kill,
gathered, the whole people;
sentences.i: that men, the whole people gathered together, are eager to kill;
sentences.n: ὅν is the relative ‘whom’, the lion; τε is the epic τε of a general statement, and καί ‘even’ goes with ἄνδρες. ἀποκτάμεναι is the epic aorist infinitive of ἀποκτείνω ‘kill’ after μεμάασιν ‘are eager’ (perfect of μέμαα). ἀγρόμενοι is the aorist middle participle of ἀγείρω ‘gather’; ἄνδρες … πᾶς δῆμος says the men are the whole people, δῆμος here ‘people’.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ πρῶτον μὲν ἀτίζων
ἔρχεται,
sentences.tr:
ho de prōton men atizōn
erchetai,
sentences.l:
but he, at first, making light of them,
goes,
sentences.i: but at first he goes on paying them no heed,
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is ‘but he’, the lion, and πρῶτον μέν ‘at first’ sets up the ἀλλ’ ὅτε ‘but when’ of the next unit. ἀτίζων is the participle of ἀτίζω ‘make light of, slight’, a rare word, and ἔρχεται ‘goes’. The simile is in the present tense, for what a lion does whenever this happens.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε κέν τις ἀρηϊθόων αἰζηῶν
δουρὶ βάλῃ ἐάλη τε χανών,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote ken tis arēïthoōn aizēōn
douri balēi ealē te chanōn,
sentences.l:
but when one of the war-swift vigorous young men
with a spear strikes, he is hemmed in, gaping,
sentences.i: but when one of the strong young men, swift in war, strikes him with a spear, he crouches, gaping,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε κέν … βάλῃ is ‘but whenever … strikes’, with ὅτε κέν and the subjunctive for what regularly happens. αἰζηός is a vigorous young man, and ἀρηϊθόων ‘swift in war’ is probably Ἄρης ‘war’ + θοός ‘swift’, though the first part is not certain. ἐάλη is the aorist passive of εἴλω ‘press together, hem in’, so the lion shrinks into himself, ‘crouches’; χανών is the aorist participle of χάσκω ‘gape’.

sentences.t:
περί τ’ ἀφρὸς ὀδόντας
γίγνεται,
sentences.tr:
peri t’ aphros odontas
gignetai,
sentences.l:
and about his teeth foam
comes to be,
sentences.i: and foam forms about his teeth,
sentences.n: περί … γίγνεται is ‘comes to be around’, with περί separated from its verb (tmesis), and ὀδόντας ‘teeth’ is its accusative. ἀφρός is ‘foam’, the froth at the mouth of the wounded lion.

sentences.t: ἐν δέ τέ οἱ κραδίῃ στένει ἄλκιμον ἦτορ,
sentences.tr: en de te hoi kradiēi stenei alkimon ētor,
sentences.l: and in his heart groans the valiant heart,
sentences.i: and in his heart the valiant heart groans,
sentences.n: The Greek has two words for ‘heart’, κραδίῃ ‘in the heart’ and ἦτορ, the subject of στένει ‘groans’, called ἄλκιμον ‘valiant’. οἱ ‘his’ (literally ‘for him’) is the lion, and τε in ἐν δέ τέ οἱ marks a general statement.

sentences.t:
οὐρῇ δὲ πλευράς τε καὶ ἰσχία ἀμφοτέρωθεν
μαστίεται,
sentences.tr:
ourēi de pleuras te kai ischia amphoterōthen
mastietai,
sentences.l:
and with his tail his sides and hips
on both sides he whips,
sentences.i: and with his tail he whips his sides and his hips, on this side and that,
sentences.n: οὐρῇ is the dative ‘with the tail’. πλευράς are the sides, the ribs, and ἰσχία the hips, and ἀμφοτέρωθεν is ‘on both sides’. μαστίεται is the present middle of μαστίω, the epic form of μαστίζω ‘whip’: the lion whips himself.

sentences.t: ἑὲ δ’ αὐτὸν ἐποτρύνει μαχέσασθαι,
sentences.tr: hee d’ auton epotrynei machesasthai,
sentences.l: and himself he urges on to fight,
sentences.i: and urges himself on to fight,
sentences.n: ἑὲ is the reflexive pronoun ‘himself’ (accusative, epic ἑ), and αὐτόν strengthens it, which the English does not repeat. ἐποτρύνει ‘urges on’ takes the aorist infinitive μαχέσασθαι ‘to fight’.

sentences.t:
γλαυκιόων δ’ ἰθὺς φέρεται μένει, ἤν τινα πέφνῃ
ἀνδρῶν, ἢ αὐτὸς φθίεται πρώτῳ ἐν ὁμίλῳ·
sentences.tr:
glaukioōn d’ ithys pheretai menei, ēn tina pephnēi
andrōn, ē autos phthietai prōtōi en homilōi·
sentences.l:
and glaring, straight on he is borne in fury, if he may kill any
of men, or himself perish in the first throng;
sentences.i: and glaring, he charges straight on in his fury, to see whether he can kill one of the men or perish himself in the foremost throng;
sentences.n: γλαυκιόων is the participle of γλαυκιάω ‘glare, gleam’, a rare verb related to γλαυκός ‘gleaming’. ἰθύς is ‘straight’, φέρεται ‘is carried, charges’, and μένει the dative of μένος, here the lion’s fury. ἤν τινα πέφνῃ ἀνδρῶν ἢ αὐτὸς φθίεται is ‘if he may kill any of the men or perish himself’, with the result left unsaid: he charges to find out which. πέφνῃ is the subjunctive of the aorist (ἔ)πεφνον ‘killed’, and φθίεται the aorist subjunctive of φθίνω ‘perish’ with a short vowel (= φθίηται), not a present.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἀχιλῆ’ ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
ἀντίον ἐλθέμεναι μεγαλήτορος Αἰνείαο.
sentences.tr:
hōs Achilē’ otryne menos kai thymos agēnōr
antion elthemenai megalētoros Aineiao.
sentences.l:
So Achilles his might and his manly spirit urged on
to go face to face with great-spirited Aeneas.
sentences.i: So his might and his proud spirit urged Achilles on to go and face great-spirited Aeneas.
sentences.n: ὣς closes the simile begun at λέων ὣς: as the lion urges himself on, so Achilles’ might and spirit urged him. Ἀχιλῆ’ is Ἀχιλῆα elided, ὄτρυνε the unaugmented imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’ (an aorist would look the same), and θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ ‘manly spirit’, ‘proud spirit’. ἐλθέμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἔρχομαι; ἀντίον … Αἰνείαο is ‘face to face with Aeneas’, with the epic genitive in -αο and the epithet μεγαλήτορος ‘great-spirited’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες,
τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē schedon ēsan ep’ allēloisin iontes,
ton proteros proseeipe podarkēs dios Achilleus·
sentences.l:
And when they were near, going against one another,
him first addressed swift-footed, heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: And when they were near, advancing on one another, swift-footed, heavenly Achilles spoke to him first:
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν … ἰόντες is ‘and when they were near, going’ (ἰόντες from εἶμι ‘go’), with ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ‘against one another’. τὸν πρότερος προσέειπε is ‘he addressed him first’; πρότερος ‘first’ is an adjective in place of an adverb. ποδάρκης ‘swift-footed’ is the epithet of Achilles; its formation is not certain, probably πούς ‘foot’ + ἀρκέω.

sentences.t:
Αἰνεία τί σὺ τόσσον ὁμίλου πολλὸν ἐπελθὼν
ἔστης;
sentences.tr:
Aineia ti sy tosson homilou pollon epelthōn
estēs;
sentences.l:
“Aeneas, why have you, so far forward of the throng, advanced
and taken your stand?
sentences.i: “Aeneas, why have you come forward so far from the throng and taken your stand?
sentences.n: Αἰνεία is the vocative. τί … ἔστης is ‘why have you taken your stand’ (ἔστης, the aorist of ἵστημι in its intransitive sense). τόσσον ὁμίλου πολλὸν ἐπελθών is ‘having advanced so far from the throng’, with τόσσον and πολλόν both stressing the distance and ὁμίλου, the genitive, the throng he has left. Achilles’ speech begins here.

sentences.l:
Does your heart bid you to fight with me,
hoping among the horse-taming Trojans to be lord
of the honour of Priam?
sentences.i: Is it your heart that bids you fight me, in the hope of being lord, among the Trojans, tamers of horses, of the honour that Priam holds?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a question, and σέ γε puts the stress on ‘you’. ἀνώγει is ‘bids’, from ἄνωγα used as a present. ἐλπόμενον ‘hoping’ agrees with σέ, and ἀνάξειν is the future infinitive of ἀνάσσω ‘be lord’, with the dative Τρώεσσιν ‘among the Trojans’ and the genitive of what he would be lord of, τιμῆς τῆς Πριάμου ‘the honour of Priam’, his standing as king, which Achilles says Aeneas hopes to take. ἱπποδάμοισι is ‘horse-taming’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ εἴ κεν ἔμ’ ἐξεναρίξῃς,
οὔ τοι τοὔνεκά γε Πρίαμος γέρας ἐν χερὶ θήσει·
sentences.tr:
atar ei ken em’ exenarixēis,
ou toi touneka ge Priamos geras en cheri thēsei·
sentences.l:
But if you despoil me,
not for you on that account indeed will Priam put a prize in your hand;
sentences.i: But if you kill me and strip me of my armour, Priam will not on that account put a prize of honour in your hand;
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ turns from the question to the fact. εἴ κεν … ἐξεναρίξῃς is ‘if you kill and strip’, κεν with the subjunctive; ἐξεναρίζω is kill an enemy and strip him of his armour (ἐνάρα ‘spoils’). οὔ τοι is ‘not to you’ (τοι = σοι), and τοὔνεκά γε is τοῦ ἕνεκα ‘on that account indeed’. γέρας is a prize of honour, and ἐν χερὶ θήσει ‘will put in your hand’.

sentences.t: εἰσὶν γάρ οἱ παῖδες, ὃ δ’ ἔμπεδος οὐδ’ ἀεσίφρων.
sentences.tr: eisin gar hoi paides, ho d’ empedos oud’ aesiphrōn.
sentences.l: for there are to him sons, and he is firm, and not senseless.
sentences.i: For he has sons, and he himself is firm and not senseless.
sentences.n: εἰσὶν … οἱ παῖδες is ‘there are to him sons’, that is, ‘he has sons’, οἱ being Priam; the point, left for the hearer to supply, is that Priam has sons of his own to follow him. ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’. ἔμπεδος ‘firm’ is paired with οὐδ’ ἀεσίφρων; ἀεσίφρων is a rare compound with φρήν ‘mind’ whose meaning is not known for certain; ‘senseless’ is the traditional guess, and the pair with ἔμπεδος ‘firm’ suits it.

sentences.t:
ἦ νύ τί τοι Τρῶες τέμενος τάμον ἔξοχον ἄλλων
καλὸν φυταλιῆς καὶ ἀρούρης,
sentences.tr:
ē ny ti toi Trōes temenos tamon exochon allōn
kalon phytaliēs kai arourēs,
sentences.l:
Or have the Trojans cut out for you some precinct, standing out above others,
fine, of planted land and of plough-land,
sentences.i: Or have the Trojans set apart for you an estate that stands out above others, a fine one of planted land and plough-land,
sentences.n: ἦ νύ τί τοι opens a second, scornful question: ‘or have the Trojans then …?’. τέμενος is a piece of land cut off and set apart, and τάμον is the epic aorist of τέμνω ‘cut’. ἔξοχον ἄλλων is ‘standing out above others’, and φυταλιῆς καὶ ἀρούρης, the genitive of respect, ‘in planted land and plough-land’ (φυταλιά ‘planted land’, ἄρουρα ‘plough-land’). These words are repeated from 6.194–195, where a precinct is cut out in the same terms.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα νέμηαι
αἴ κεν ἐμὲ κτείνῃς;
sentences.tr:
ophra nemēai
ai ken eme kteinēis;
sentences.l:
that you may occupy it,
if you kill me?
sentences.i: for you to occupy, if you kill me?
sentences.n: ὄφρα νέμηαι is a purpose clause: νέμομαι is ‘hold and use’, so ‘occupy’ (of land), and νέμηαι is the subjunctive with the epic ending -ηαι (Attic νέμῃ). αἴ is εἰ ‘if’ before κεν, and κτείνῃς the subjunctive of κτείνω ‘kill’.

sentences.t: χαλεπῶς δέ σ’ ἔολπα τὸ ῥέξειν.
sentences.tr: chalepōs de s’ eolpa to rhexein.
sentences.l: and with difficulty, I expect, you will do this.
sentences.i: But I expect you will do it only with difficulty.
sentences.n: ἔολπα is a perfect with present sense, ‘I expect’ (from ἔλπομαι). σ’ (σε) is the subject of ῥέξειν, the future infinitive of ῥέζω ‘do’, and τὸ ‘this’ is the killing of Achilles. χαλεπῶς is the adverb of χαλεπός, ‘with difficulty’.

sentences.t: ἤδη μὲν σέ γέ φημι καὶ ἄλλοτε δουρὶ φοβῆσαι.
sentences.tr: ēdē men se ge phēmi kai allote douri phobēsai.
sentences.l: Already, I say, I have put you to flight at another time too, with my spear.
sentences.i: I say that before now, on another occasion, I put you to flight with my spear.
sentences.n: φημί ‘I say’ takes the aorist infinitive φοβῆσαι (φοβέω ‘put to flight’), with σέ as its object. ἤδη μέν is ‘already indeed’, καὶ ἄλλοτε ‘at another time too’, and δουρί the dative of δόρυ ‘spear’. The occasion is told in the next lines.

sentences.l:
Do you not remember when I drove you from the cattle, alone as you were,
down from the Idaean mountains on quick feet,
swiftly?
sentences.i: Do you not remember how I drove you down from the Idaean mountains, away from your cattle, all alone, on quick feet and swiftly?
sentences.n: μέμνῃ is μέμνησαι ‘you remember’ (the perfect of μιμνῄσκομαι, present in sense). ὅτε πέρ is ‘when indeed’. βοῶν ἄπο is ‘away from the cattle’, with ἄπο placed after its noun; μοῦνον ἐόντα ‘being alone’. σεῦα is the unaugmented aorist of σεύω ‘chase, drive’, and κατ’ Ἰδαίων ὀρέων ‘down from the Idaean mountains’, the mountains of Ida. ταχέεσσι πόδεσσι is ‘on quick feet’, the Greek not saying whose; καρπαλίμως ‘swiftly’.

sentences.t: τότε δ’ οὔ τι μετατροπαλίζεο φεύγων.
sentences.tr: tote d’ ou ti metatropalizeo pheugōn.
sentences.l: and then in no way did you keep turning round, fleeing.
sentences.i: and as you fled then you did not keep turning round.
sentences.n: μετατροπαλίζεο is the imperfect of μετατροπαλίζομαι ‘keep turning round’, a frequentative built on τρέπω ‘turn’, with the epic ending -εο (Attic -ου). οὔ τι is ‘in no way’, and φεύγων ‘fleeing’.

sentences.t: ἔνθεν δ’ ἐς Λυρνησσὸν ὑπέκφυγες·
sentences.tr: enthen d’ es Lyrnēsson hypekphyges·
sentences.l: And from there to Lyrnessus you escaped;
sentences.i: From there you escaped to Lyrnessus;
sentences.n: ἔνθεν is ‘from there’, the mountain slopes just named. Λυρνησσός is a town; the next lines say Achilles sacked it. ὑπέκφυγες is the aorist of ὑπεκφεύγω ‘escape from under’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ τὴν
πέρσα μεθορμηθεὶς σὺν Ἀθήνῃ καὶ Διὶ πατρί,
sentences.tr:
autar egō tēn
persa methormētheis syn Athēnēi kai Dii patri,
sentences.l:
but I it
sacked, having set out in pursuit, with Athena and father Zeus,
sentences.i: but I set out in pursuit and sacked it, with Athena and father Zeus,
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’. τήν is ‘it’, the city, put before the verb for emphasis, and πέρσα is the epic aorist of πέρθω ‘sack’. μεθορμηθείς is the aorist passive participle of μεθορμάομαι ‘set out’ (μετά + ὁρμάω ‘set in motion’); the μετά may mean ‘after’, and the Greek does not say after whom or what. σὺν Ἀθήνῃ καὶ Διὶ πατρί is ‘with Athena and father Zeus’.

sentences.t:
ληϊάδας δὲ γυναῖκας ἐλεύθερον ἦμαρ ἀπούρας
ἦγον·
sentences.tr:
lēïadas de gynaikas eleutheron ēmar apouras
ēgon·
sentences.l:
and the women taken as spoil, the day of freedom having taken away,
I led off;
sentences.i: and I led off the women taken as spoil, having taken from them the day of freedom;
sentences.n: ληϊάδας is an adjective formed on ληΐς ‘booty’, so ‘women taken as spoil’. ἐλεύθερον ἦμαρ ἀπούρας is ‘having taken away the day of freedom’, the same picture as the ‘day of slavery’ said of a captive woman elsewhere. ἀπούρας is the aorist participle of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’, and ἦγον ‘led off’.

sentences.t: ἀτὰρ σὲ Ζεὺς ἐρρύσατο καὶ θεοὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.tr: atar se Zeus errysato kai theoi alloi.
sentences.l: but you Zeus rescued, and the other gods.
sentences.i: but Zeus rescued you, and the other gods.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’. ἐρρύσατο is the aorist middle of ῥύομαι ‘rescue, protect’, with Zeus as subject and καὶ θεοὶ ἄλλοι ‘and the other gods’ added after the verb; σέ ‘you’ stands first for stress.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐ νῦν ἐρύεσθαι ὀΐομαι, ὡς ἐνὶ θυμῷ
βάλλεαι·
sentences.tr:
all’ ou nyn eryesthai oïomai, hōs eni thymōi
balleai·
sentences.l:
But not now to rescue, I think, as in your heart
you cast;
sentences.i: But I do not think you will be rescued now, as you suppose in your heart;
sentences.n: ἐρύεσθαι is the infinitive of ἐρύομαι ‘rescue, protect’, another form of ῥύομαι, the verb of ἐρρύσατο in the line before; the Greek leaves out who rescues and whom, and the English takes ‘you will be rescued’. ὀΐομαι is ‘I think’. ὡς ἐνὶ θυμῷ βάλλεαι is ‘as you cast in your heart’, that is, as you suppose; βάλλεαι is the epic second singular middle of βάλλω.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά σ’ ἔγωγ’ ἀναχωρήσαντα κελεύω
ἐς πληθὺν ἰέναι, μηδ’ ἀντίος ἵστασ’ ἐμεῖο,
πρίν τι κακὸν παθέειν· ῥεχθὲν δέ τε νήπιος ἔγνω.
sentences.tr:
alla s’ egōg’ anachōrēsanta keleuō
es plēthyn ienai, mēd’ antios histas’ emeio,
prin ti kakon patheein· rhechthen de te nēpios egnō.
sentences.l:
but I, for my part, bid you, stepping back,
to go into the crowd, and not to stand opposite me
before suffering some evil; a thing done a foolish one learns.”
sentences.i: But I, for my part, bid you step back into the crowd, and not stand to face me before you suffer some harm; even a foolish man learns when the thing is done.”
sentences.n: ἀναχωρήσαντα, the aorist participle of ἀναχωρέω ‘step back’, agrees with σέ, the object of κελεύω ‘I bid’, which takes the infinitive ἰέναι ‘to go’; μηδ’ … ἵστασ’ is the prohibition ‘and do not take your stand’, with ἀντίος ‘opposite’ and ἐμεῖο, the epic genitive of ἐγώ. πρίν τι κακὸν παθέειν is πρίν with the epic infinitive, ‘before suffering some evil’. ῥεχθέν ‘a thing done’ (aorist passive of ῥέζω) is the object of ἔγνω, a gnomic aorist: a foolish man learns only after the deed. The same lines stand at 17.30–32. Achilles’ speech ends here.
